title: Elixir Quick Reference
description: Look up a lesson idea, see its small example, and check a common mistake. Open the linked lesson for setup and practice steps.

entries.name: Print a greeting
entries.summary: IO.puts writes text and adds a newline. IO means input and output.

entries.name: Name a value
entries.summary: A name can be bound to a value. The plus sign adds numbers.
notes: Values are not changed in place; a new binding is different from mutation.

entries.name: Name a fixed label
entries.summary: An atom is a named label. It begins with a colon and is often used for a small set of choices.
notes: Do not create unlimited new atoms from user input.

entries.name: Keep a small group
entries.summary: A tuple groups a few values. It is often used to return a status and a result together.

entries.name: Store a sequence
entries.summary: A list holds a sequence of values. Enum.join turns these strings into one string.
notes: Lists and tuples are different data shapes.

entries.name: Use named fields
entries.summary: A map stores key-value pairs. Atom keys can be read with dot syntax.
notes: A missing key with dot syntax raises an error.

entries.name: Pull values from a shape
entries.summary: The equals sign matches shapes and binds names to their parts.
notes: A shape that does not match raises a match error.

entries.name: Choose with if
entries.summary: if picks one of two branches. Only false and nil count as false in Elixir.

example.code:
score = 8
IO.puts(if score >= 5, do: "Pass", else: "Try again")

notes: Zero is a true value, so test a number with an explicit rule.

entries.name: Use an anonymous function
entries.summary: fn creates a function value. A dot is used when calling a function stored in a variable.

example.code:
twice = fn n -> n * 2 end
IO.puts(twice.(4))

notes: Do not omit the dot in this kind of function call.

entries.name: Transform each value
entries.summary: Enum.map builds a list using the result of a function for each item.

example.code:
values = Enum.map([2, 3], fn n -> n * 2 end)
IO.puts(Enum.join(values, ", "))

notes: Keep the returned list if you need it later.

entries.name: Read steps from left to right
entries.summary: The pipe |> passes a value as the first input to the next function.

example.code:
[4, 8, 9]
|> Enum.filter(fn n -> n >= 7 end)
|> Enum.sum()
|> IO.puts()

notes: The piped value becomes the first argument, not the last.

entries.name: Choose by a pattern
entries.summary: case matches a value against patterns. _ is a catch-all pattern.

example.code:
result = {:ok, 8}
message = case result do
 {:ok, n} -> "Score: #{n}"
 _ -> "Try again"
end
IO.puts(message)

notes: Include a case for the shapes your program can receive.
